intro: Eusebius of Caesarea, writing his Church History in Greek around AD 324, records a correspondence he says he translated from Syriac documents in the archives of Edessa: a letter from King Abgar of Edessa to Jesus, and Jesus’ reply.

excerpts.text: Abgarus, ruler of Edessa, to Jesus the excellent Saviour who has appeared in the country of Jerusalem, greeting. I have heard the reports of thee and of thy cures as performed by thee without medicines or herbs. For it is said that thou makest the blind to see and the lame to walk, that thou cleansest lepers and castest out impure spirits and demons, and that thou healest those afflicted with lingering disease, and raisest the dead. … I have therefore written to thee to ask thee that thou wouldest take the trouble to come to me and heal the disease which I have. For I have heard that the Jews are murmuring against thee and are plotting to injure thee. But I have a very small yet noble city which is great enough for us both.

Blessed art thou who hast believed in me without having seen me. For it is written concerning me, that they who have seen me will not believe in me, and that they who have not seen me will believe and be saved. But in regard to what thou hast written me, that I should come to thee, it is necessary for me to fulfill all things here for which I have been sent, and after I have fulfilled them thus to be taken up again to him that sent me. But after I have been taken up I will send to thee one of my disciples, that he may heal thy disease and give life to thee and thine.
excerpts.cite: Eusebius, Church History I.13.10 (the reply of Jesus)

note: Scholars regard the letters as a legend that took shape in Edessa by the third century, but they were treasured across the Syriac-speaking East. Armenian tradition cherishes Abgar as its own — Moses of Khorene retells the story at length, and the Armenian Church honors Abgar as a saint.

intro: In 1897 Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt dug a torn papyrus leaf out of the rubbish mounds of Oxyrhynchus, Egypt — a Greek page of “Sayings of Jesus” copied around AD 200. They rushed it into print the same year as ΛΟΓΙΑ ΙΗΣΟΥ: Sayings of Our Lord.

excerpts.text: Jesus saith, Wherever there are .... and there is one .... alone, I am with him. Raise the stone and there thou shalt find me, cleave the wood and there am I.
excerpts.cite: P.Oxy. I 1, Logion 5 (gaps mark holes in the papyrus)
excerpts.translator: Bernard P. Grenfell & Arthur S. Hunt (1897)

excerpts.text: Jesus saith, A prophet is not acceptable in his own country, neither doth a physician work cures upon them that know him.
excerpts.translator: Bernard P. Grenfell & Arthur S. Hunt (1897)

excerpts.text: Jesus saith, A city built upon the top of a high hill, and stablished, can neither fall nor be hid.
excerpts.translator: Bernard P. Grenfell & Arthur S. Hunt (1897)

note: After the Coptic Gospel of Thomas surfaced at Nag Hammadi in 1945, these papyrus sayings were identified as fragments of a Greek Thomas. The full Coptic text has no public-domain English translation, so it is linked here rather than quoted.

linkOut.label: Gospel of Thomas — Coptic texts and scholarship (Brill)

intro: The Protoevangelium of James is a Greek infancy gospel from the second century, telling of Mary’s childhood and of the birth of Jesus in a cave near Bethlehem. It was never received into the New Testament canon, yet it shaped Christian devotion and art, East and West.

excerpts.text: And they stood in the place of the cave, and behold a luminous cloud overshadowed the cave. And the midwife said: My soul has been magnified this day, because mine eyes have seen strange things … And immediately the cloud disappeared out of the cave, and a great light shone in the cave, so that the eyes could not bear it. And in a little that light gradually decreased, until the infant appeared, and went and took the breast from His mother Mary.
excerpts.translator: Alexander Walker, Ante-Nicene Fathers Vol. VIII (1886)

note: Though ascribed to James, the brother of Jesus, scholars date the work to the mid-second century. It is the earliest source for the names of Mary’s parents, Joachim and Anna, and for the tradition of the birth-cave.

intro: The Quran, the scripture of Islam delivered in Arabic in the seventh century, presents Jesus — ʿIsa, son of Mary — as one of God’s greatest prophets and messengers: born of a virgin, working miracles by God’s leave, and titled Messiah and “Word from Him.”

excerpts.text: Remember when the angel said, "O Mary! Verily God announceth to thee the Word from Him: His name shall be, Messiah Jesus the son of Mary … And He shall speak to men alike when in the cradle and when grown up; And he shall be one of the just." She said, "How, O my Lord! shall I have a son, when man hath not touched me?" He said, "Thus: God will create what He will; When He decreeth a thing, He only saith, 'Be,' and it is."
excerpts.cite: Quran, Sura III (“The Family of Imran”), 45–47

excerpts.text: And make mention in the Book, of Mary, when she went apart from her family, eastward … And she made a sign to them, pointing towards the babe. They said, "How shall we speak with him who is in the cradle, an infant?" … "Verily, I am the servant of God; He hath given me the Book, and He hath made me a prophet; And He hath made me blessed wherever I may be, and hath enjoined me prayer and almsgiving so long as I shall live …

And for their saying, "Verily we have slain the Messiah, Jesus the son of Mary, an Apostle of God." Yet they slew him not, and they crucified him not, but they had only his likeness … they did not really slay him, but God took him up to Himself. And God is Mighty, Wise!

note: Islam affirms Jesus’ virgin birth, miracles, and return, but not his divinity or death on the cross — Sura 4:157 states “they slew him not,” and most Muslim interpreters hold that God raised Jesus alive to himself. Rodwell’s 1861 translation, quoted here, arranges the suras in his own chronological order.

intro: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, Christian since the fourth century, keeps its scriptures and services in Geʿez and preserves a broader biblical canon than any other church.
note: One of its treasured books about Jesus, read aloud on feast days, is the Taʼamra Iyasus (“Miracles of Jesus”) — compiled in Geʿez around the fourteenth century from Arabic sources that drew in turn on Syriac tradition. Its distinctive material has no public-domain English translation, so none is quoted here; the manuscript below is linked instead.
